title: Budget versus actual with a variance flag

docs.syntax: =ROUND((actual-budget)/budget,3) sizes the variance; ABS lets one threshold catch both directions
docs.explain: A budget report is only useful when it says which lines need attention, and the arithmetic that makes the decision is a division rather than a subtraction. Dividing by the budget turns a variance into a share of what was planned. That is what makes one threshold apply to every line: twenty pounds over is nothing on a five thousand pound line and everything on a fifty pound one. The first screen writes that share and rounds it. An unrounded ratio is a long tail of digits that nobody reads, and no comparison against a threshold can be written to match it. The second screen adds the flag, and the interesting part is the ABS call. A flag written without it catches overspends and silently lets underspends through, so a line thirty per cent under budget never gets reviewed. Wrapping the difference in ABS makes one threshold cover both directions, which is what a review flag is for. Together the two screens are the shape of every variance table: a share of plan, then a word that says whether that share is worth a conversation.

errors.text: The budget figure is zero, so the variance has nothing to be measured against.
A budget or actual cell holds text, so the difference cannot be worked out.

docs.atWork: Turning budget and actual columns into a comparable variance and a review flag.
docs.outcome: Size a variance as a share of budget, then flag it with one threshold in both directions.
docs.teaches: a rounded variance share, then an IF over ABS so under- and overspends both flag
docs.dataset: Four budget lines with budget, actual and one answer cell

screens.prompt: In D2, report the actual-vs-budget variance of the first line as a share of its budget, to three decimal places.

hints.syntax: =ROUND((C2-B2)/B2,3): the difference over the budget, to three places.
hints.func-round: The raw ratio is a long tail of digits, so it is rounded for reporting.
hints.require-ref: The budget figure is in B2.
hints.value: A hundred over two thousand is five per cent, or 0.05.
hints.error: A zero budget leaves the share nothing to be measured against.

reject.why: the difference is left as an amount rather than a share
a hundred pounds is not five per cent
the subtraction runs the wrong way, giving a negative share
the difference is measured against the actual rather than the budget
the formula reads the second line rather than B2
the difference is divided by zero
the arguments fall outside the parentheses

screens.prompt: In D2, flag the first line review when its variance is more than ten per cent in either direction and ok otherwise.

hints.syntax: =IF(ABS(C2-B2)/B2>0.1,"review","ok"): the absolute share against the threshold, then two words.
hints.func-if: The cell has to choose between two words.
hints.func-abs: An overspend and an underspend both count, so the difference is taken without its sign.
hints.require-ref: The budget figure is in B2.
hints.value: Five per cent is inside ten, so the first line is ok.
hints.error: A zero budget divides by zero before the comparison is made.

reject.why: the flag is typed rather than decided by the variance
the size of the variance never enters, so any overspend flags
a hundred pounds is compared against a share
the formula reads the second line rather than B2
the difference is divided by zero inside the test
the arguments fall outside the parentheses

seo.title: Budget versus actual with a variance flag
seo.description: A variance divided by its budget lets one threshold fit every line. ABS around the difference catches underspends too, so nothing slips past review.
